# Review

## What Our LPs Assumed

- **Divisibility**: any fraction of a decision is allowed.
- Economic dispatch assumed every plant was **already on**.

**Raises the question**: how do we model decisions that are **on or off**?

# Discrete Decisions

## Problems With Discrete Decisions

Some decisions can't be divided into fractions.

- **Which generators to run** this hour, not just how much?
- Whether to **build** a facility at all?
- How many **trucks**, pumps, or treatment units?

::: {.notes}
Economic dispatch took the set of running plants as given. In practice, operators also decide which plants to switch on, and a plant that's on has to produce at least its minimum and costs money just to keep running. Facility siting has the same structure: a site is either built or not.
:::

## Fixed Costs Cause Discontinuities

::: {#6 .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"}
units = 1:10
total_cost(x) = 3 + 2x                       # fixed cost 3, variable cost 2 per unit
p_fixed = plot(units, total_cost.(units), color=:black, marker=:circle, label="total cost",
    xlabel="Units of operation", ylabel="Cost", xticks=0:10, xlims=(-0.5, 10.5),
    ylims=(-0.5, 24), legend=:topleft, framestyle=:origin)
plot!(p_fixed, units, total_cost.(units) ./ units, color=cb_vermillion, linestyle=:dot,
    label="average cost per unit")
scatter!(p_fixed, [0], [0], color=:black, markersize=6)
plot!(p_fixed, size=(1200, 330), left_margin=10mm, bottom_margin=14mm)
```

A **fixed cost** to operate at all, plus a **variable cost** per unit, makes the cost jump at zero.

::: {.notes}
Operating costs nothing at zero output, then jumps to the fixed cost as soon as anything is produced. That jump can't be written as a linear function of output alone, and the falling average cost (the dotted line) is why fixed costs push toward running fewer, larger operations.
:::

## Binary Variables

An **indicator** variable flags whether something is on:

$$u_g = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{off} \\ 1 & \text{on} \end{cases}$$

More generally, **integer** variables $x \in \mathbb{Z}$: numbers of units, trucks, or turbines.

A linear program with some integer variables is a **mixed integer (linear) program**, a MILP.

::: {.notes}
Binary variables are integer variables restricted to 0 and 1. With them we can write fixed costs and on/off logic as linear expressions, at the price of losing divisibility.
:::

# Modelling With Binaries

## Which Plants Should Run?

``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"}
plants = ["Coal", "CCGT", "CT"]
min_output = [100, 50, 0]           # [MW] when on
max_output = [250, 200, 100]        # [MW]
marginal_cost = [20, 30, 50]        # [$/MWh]
fixed_cost = [3000, 1000, 100]      # [$/h] when on
println("| Plant | Minimum (MW) | Maximum (MW) | Marginal cost (\\\$/MWh) | Fixed cost when on (\\\$/h) |")
println("|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|")
for i in 1:3
    println("| $(plants[i]) | $(min_output[i]) | $(max_output[i]) | $(marginal_cost[i]) | $(commas(fixed_cost[i])) |")
end
```
| Plant | Minimum (MW) | Maximum (MW) | Marginal cost (\$/MWh) | Fixed cost when on (\$/h) |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Coal | 100 | 250 | 20 | 3,000 |
| CCGT | 50 | 200 | 30 | 1,000 |
| CT | 0 | 100 | 50 | 100 |



Demand is **150 MW**. Which plants should run?

::: {.notes}
Let students guess. The merit-order instinct from dispatch says coal: it has the cheapest energy. But coal has the largest fixed cost, and its minimum output is 100 MW. Hold the answer until the JuMP slide.
:::

## Linking Output to On/Off

Write the problem with binaries $u_i$ and outputs $y_i$.

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
$$
\begin{aligned}
\min_{\mathbf{y}, \mathbf{u}} \quad & \sum_i \left(\text{FixedCost}_i \, u_i + \text{MarginalCost}_i \, y_i\right) \\
\text{subject to:} \quad & \sum_i y_i \geq d \\[0.3em]
& y_i \leq P^{\text{max}}_i \, u_i \qquad \text{(no output when off)} \\[0.3em]
& y_i \geq P^{\text{min}}_i \, u_i \qquad \text{(at least the minimum when on)} \\[0.3em]
& u_i \in \{0, 1\}, \ y_i \geq 0
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

::: {.notes}
Board item; the fragment is the answer. The key move is the linking constraint: multiply the capacity by the binary. When u is 0, the plant's output is forced to zero; when u is 1, it can run between its minimum and maximum. The fixed cost is paid only when u is 1. The same pattern (capacity times a binary) switches facilities on and off in facility siting and network models.
:::

## The Three-Plant Model in `JuMP`

::: {#10 .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="false"}
function commit(demand; relax=false)
    model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
    @variable(model, y[1:3] >= 0)            # output [MW]
    @variable(model, u[1:3], Bin)            # on or off
    @objective(model, Min, sum(fixed_cost .* u) + sum(marginal_cost .* y))
    @constraint(model, sum(y) >= demand)
    @constraint(model, [i in 1:3], y[i] <= max_output[i] * u[i])
    @constraint(model, [i in 1:3], y[i] >= min_output[i] * u[i])
    if relax
        relax_integrality(model)             # drop integrality: an LP
    end
    set_silent(model)
    optimize!(model)
    return (output=value.(y), on=value.(u), cost=objective_value(model))
end
```
:::



::: {.notes}
`Bin` declares a binary variable. The rest is an ordinary LP model. The `relax` option is for later in the lecture.
:::

## Why Not Coal?




At 150 MW the cheapest plan runs the **CCGT alone**, at \$5,500/h, although coal's energy is cheapest. When does coal win?

::: {.fragment .fade-in}
- Coal alone: $3{,}000 + 20 \times 150 =$ \$6,000/h.
- CCGT alone: $1{,}000 + 30 \times 150 =$ \$5,500/h.
- $3{,}000 + 20d = 1{,}000 + 30d$: coal wins above **200 MW**.
:::

::: {.notes}
Board item; the fragments carry the working. Coal saves 10 dollars per MWh but costs 2,000 dollars an hour more to switch on, so it pays only above 200 MW. Above 250 MW coal is full and something else has to top it up; at 280 MW the MIP picks the CT, not the CCGT, because the CCGT would have to run at least 50 MW and pay its 1,000 dollar fixed cost: another case where the fixed cost, not the marginal cost, decides.
:::

## Logical Constraints

Binaries also encode rules between decisions:

| Rule | Constraint |
|:--|:--|
| at most one of CCGT and CT | $u_2 + u_3 \leq 1$ |
| CT only if coal runs | $u_3 \leq u_1$ |
| either $\mathbf{a}^\top \mathbf{y} \leq b_1$ or $\mathbf{c}^\top \mathbf{y} \leq b_2$ | $\mathbf{a}^\top \mathbf{y} \leq b_1 + M z$, $\ \mathbf{c}^\top \mathbf{y} \leq b_2 + M(1 - z)$ |

$z$ is binary; $M$ is big enough to switch one off ("big-$M$").

::: {.notes}
These are patterns, not results: in this example the at-most-one rule doesn't change the answer at any demand we tried. The either/or (disjunctive) form uses one binary to choose which of two constraints holds; M has to be big enough to make the other constraint non-binding, and no bigger than necessary, because a huge M makes the LP relaxation weak.
:::

# The LP Relaxation

## Relaxing the Binary Variables

``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"}
lp_150 = commit(150; relax=true)
demands = [150, 220, 280, 420]
mip_cost = zeros(length(demands))
lp_cost = zeros(length(demands))
for (k, d) in enumerate(demands)
    mip_cost[k] = commit(d).cost
    lp_cost[k] = commit(d; relax=true).cost
end
println("| Demand (MW) | MIP (\\\$/h) | LP relaxation (\\\$/h) | Gap |")
println("|--:|--:|--:|--:|")
for k in eachindex(demands)
    println("| $(demands[k]) | $(commas(mip_cost[k])) | $(commas(lp_cost[k])) | $(round(100 * (mip_cost[k] - lp_cost[k]) / mip_cost[k]; digits=1))% |")
end
```
| Demand (MW) | MIP (\$/h) | LP relaxation (\$/h) | Gap |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 150 | 5,500 | 4,800 | 12.7% |
| 220 | 7,400 | 7,040 | 4.9% |
| 280 | 9,600 | 9,050 | 5.7% |
| 420 | 14,100 | 13,950 | 1.1% |



At 150 MW the relaxation runs coal **60% on**.

::: {.notes}
relax_integrality turns the binaries into continuous variables between 0 and 1. The relaxed problem pays only 60% of coal's fixed cost for running 60% of its capacity, which no real plant can do. In effect each plant costs its marginal cost plus its fixed cost spread over its maximum output: coal 32, CCGT 35, CT 51 dollars per MWh, so the relaxation always fills coal first. The gap is largest at low demand, where the MIP pays a whole fixed cost for a part-loaded plant, and smallest at 420 MW, where the plants it runs are nearly full; at 280 MW it widens a little because the MIP tops up full coal with the CT.
:::

## Why the Relaxation Is a Bound

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width=50%}

::: {#16 .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"}
xs = 2:0.05:10.75
upper_edge(x) = min(4.5x, 16 - x)
lower_edge(x) = max(12 - 1.5x, 0.5x)
p_div = plot(xs, lower_edge.(xs), fillrange=upper_edge.(xs), color=cb_sky, alpha=0.5,
    linewidth=0, xlabel=L"x_1", ylabel=L"x_2", xlims=(0, 12), ylims=(0, 15), framestyle=:origin)
# mark the integer points inside the region
for i in 2:10
    for j in 0:15
        if lower_edge(i) <= j <= upper_edge(i)
            scatter!(p_div, [i], [j], color=:black, markersize=4)
        end
    end
end
plot!(p_div, size=(600, 500), left_margin=8mm)
```

The integer points are a **subset** of the LP's region, so the relaxed optimum is:

- a **lower bound** when minimizing;
- an **upper bound** when maximizing.
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The shaded region is an LP's feasible region; the dots are the integer points inside it. Dropping integrality can only add options, so the relaxed optimum is never worse than the integer optimum. For a minimization (like our plants) that makes it a lower bound on cost; for a maximization (the next example) an upper bound. LP corners land on integer points only by luck, which is why we can't just solve the LP and round.
:::

# Branch and Bound

## A Simple MILP

$$
\begin{aligned}
\max \quad & 3x_1 + 4x_2 \\
\text{subject to:} \quad & 2x_1 + 6x_2 \leq 27 \\
& x_2 \geq 2 \\
& 3x_1 + x_2 \leq 19 \\
& x_1, x_2 \geq 0, \ \text{integer}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Branch and bound**: solve LP relaxations, split on a fractional variable, and prune branches that can't beat the best integer solution found so far.

::: {.notes}
This example maximizes, so the relaxation gives an upper bound. Any integer point we find gives a lower bound. Branch and bound narrows the gap between them.
:::

## Node 1: The LP Relaxation

::: {#18 .cell execution_count=1}
``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"}
# Solve the LP relaxation at a node, given extra bounds from branching
function node_lp(; x1_max=Inf, x1_min=0, x2_max=Inf, x2_min=2)
    model = Model(HiGHS.Optimizer)
    @variable(model, x1_min <= x1 <= x1_max)
    @variable(model, x2_min <= x2 <= x2_max)
    @objective(model, Max, 3x1 + 4x2)
    @constraint(model, 2x1 + 6x2 <= 27)
    @constraint(model, 3x1 + x2 <= 19)
    set_silent(model)
    optimize!(model)
    if !is_solved_and_feasible(model)
        return nothing                       # the node is infeasible
    end
    return (x1=value(x1), x2=value(x2), z=objective_value(model))
end

# Draw the region allowed at a node, its integer points, and its LP optimum
function node_plot(; x1_max=Inf, x1_min=0, x2_max=Inf, x2_min=2, title="")
    p = plot(xlabel=L"x_1", ylabel=L"x_2", xlims=(0, 6), ylims=(0, 5), framestyle=:origin,
        xticks=0:6, yticks=0:5, title=title)
    # shade the region allowed at this node
    xs = range(max(0, x1_min), min(6, x1_max); length=200)
    top_edge = zeros(length(xs))
    for k in eachindex(xs)
        top_edge[k] = min((27 - 2xs[k]) / 6, 19 - 3xs[k], x2_max)
    end
    inside = top_edge .>= x2_min
    if any(inside)
        plot!(p, xs[inside], fill(x2_min, count(inside)), fillrange=top_edge[inside],
            color=cb_sky, alpha=0.5, linewidth=0)
    end
    plot!(p, 0:0.1:6, (27 .- 2 .* (0:0.1:6)) ./ 6, color=cb_purple)
    plot!(p, 0:0.1:6, 19 .- 3 .* (0:0.1:6), color=cb_blue, linestyle=:dash)
    hline!(p, [2], color=cb_vermillion, linestyle=:dashdot)
    # mark the integer points allowed at this node
    for i in 0:6
        for j in 2:5
            if 2i + 6j <= 27 && 3i + j <= 19 && x1_min <= i <= x1_max && x2_min <= j <= x2_max
                scatter!(p, [i], [j], color=:black, markersize=6)
            end
        end
    end
    sol = node_lp(x1_max=x1_max, x1_min=x1_min, x2_max=x2_max, x2_min=x2_min)
    if !isnothing(sol)
        scatter!(p, [sol.x1], [sol.x2], color=cb_yellow, markersize=11,
            markerstrokecolor=:black, markerstrokewidth=2)
    end
    return p, sol
end

# Objective values to two places, with no decimals on whole numbers
function show_z(z)
    z_two_places = round(z; digits=2)
    if isinteger(z_two_places)
        return string(round(Int, z_two_places))
    end
    return string(z_two_places)
end

# A node's objective, or "infeasible"
function show_node(sol)
    if isnothing(sol)
        return "infeasible"
    end
    return show_z(sol.z)
end

p1, node1 = node_plot()
rounded = (floor(Int, node1.x1), floor(Int, node1.x2))    # round the LP point down
rounded_z = 3 * rounded[1] + 4 * rounded[2]
plot!(p1, size=(1100, 300), left_margin=8mm)
```

Board item: draw the two child problems as branches from node 1, with their bounds. Every integer point lies in one branch or the other, because no integer lies strictly between 2 and 3. The bounds can only get worse as we go down the tree.
:::

``` {.julia .cell-code code-fold="true"}
# Edges, from the bottom of each parent's box to the top of its child's
for k in 2:9
    j = parent[k]
    plot!(p_tree, [node_x[j], node_x[k]], [node_y[j] - half_height, node_y[k] + half_height],
        color=:gray40, linewidth=2)
    mid_x = (node_x[j] + node_x[k]) / 2
    mid_y = (node_y[j] + node_y[k]) / 2
    if node_x[k] < node_x[j]
        annotate!(p_tree, mid_x - 0.12, mid_y, text(branch[k], 17, :right))

end
# A box for each node: its LP result and what happened to it

    sol = tree_nodes[k]
    if isnothing(sol)
        top_line = "Node $(k)"
        bottom_line = "infeasible"

        bottom_line = "($(show_z(sol.x1)), $(show_z(sol.x2)))"
        if outcome[k] != ""

    if isnothing(sol) || outcome[k] == "pruned"
        box_color = :gray70                        # the branch ends here
    elseif outcome[k] == "incumbent" || outcome[k] == "optimum"
        box_color = cb_green                       # an integer solution

    box_y = node_y[k] .+ [-half_height, -half_height, half_height, half_height]
    plot!(p_tree, Shape(box_x, box_y), fillcolor=box_color, fillalpha=0.35,
        linecolor=:black, linewidth=1.5)
    annotate!(p_tree, node_x[k], node_y[k] + 0.14, text(top_line, 17, plot_font))
    annotate!(p_tree, node_x[k], node_y[k] - 0.15, text(bottom_line, 17, plot_font))
```

::: {.notes}
Green boxes are integer solutions; grey boxes end a branch. Prune a branch when it is infeasible, when it gives an integer solution (nothing below can do better), or when its bound is worse than the incumbent. Node 6 is the first incumbent; node 8 beats it; node 9's bound is below node 8's value. Nodes 4 through 9 are worked in the appendix, solved by the same function. In the worst case the tree grows exponentially with the number of integer variables, which is why commercial solvers add cutting planes and heuristics (branch and cut).
:::

# Key Takeaways and Upcoming Schedule

## Key Takeaways

::: {.incremental}
- **Binary variables** turn on/off decisions into linear constraints: fixed cost × $u$, output ≤ capacity × $u$.
- **Fixed costs can overturn the merit order**: a plant with cheaper energy can lose to one that costs less to switch on.
- The **LP relaxation** bounds the MIP (below for min, above for max), but its "solution" can be meaningless.
- **Branch and bound** solves relaxations, branches on fractional variables, and prunes.
:::
